desc:
Encoding. A non-negative integer is stored as an array of its decimal digits, most significant digit first, one digit per element, with no leading zeros; the number zero is stored as [0]. Results use the same format. The numbers can have thousands of digits, so you cannot convert a whole array into one machine integer.

nums is a list of big numbers, each stored as a digit array (the arrays may have different lengths). Return the digit array of their sum.

Example: nums = [[9,9],[9,9],[1]] (99 + 99 + 1) gives [1,9,9]. Example: nums = [[5],[0]] gives [5].
constraints: 0 ≤ nums[i][j] ≤ 9, no leading zeros in a number except for [0]
hints: Adding the numbers one after another with a two-number addition works, but think about doing all of them in a single pass.
Align all numbers on the right. Column sums can be larger than 9 by a lot (up to 9 × 200 plus a carry), so a carry is no longer just 0 or 1.

First add up every column into one array of column sums (index from the right end). Then sweep once from the right: digit = (sum + carry) % 10, carry = (sum + carry) // 10, and flush the leftover carry at the end.
editorial: Let W be the longest length. Create an array cols of W column sums where position W-1 is the units column. For each number, add its digits into the columns aligned to the right (a number of length L starts at column W-L).

Then perform a single carry sweep from the units column: v = cols[p] + carry, output v % 10, carry v // 10. The carry can be several digits wide (at most about 1,800 here), so after the last column keep emitting digits while the carry is positive. Reverse the output. The total work is O(total number of digits) with a single carry sweep, instead of one full carry pass per added number.
